title: Restaurant Order System
story: Friday night. The restaurant is packed. Orders are flying in — appetizers, mains, desserts, drinks. You're not a waiter; you built the system that handles it all. Browse the menu by category, add items to your cart, see the running total, and at checkout, a surprise: spend over $50 and get 10% off. Print a crisp receipt with every item, subtotal, discount, and final total. You just built a POS system.
why: The Restaurant Order System models a real-world transactional application with enums for categories, structs for items and orders, Vec for cart, Map for category grouping, and discount calculation with contracts — a complete ordering engine.
analogy: A restaurant POS terminal at the counter. The menu is the laminated card with prices. The cart is the server's notepad — scribble items as they're ordered. Running total updates with each addition. At checkout, the cash register applies promotions (10% off orders over $50), adds tax, and prints a receipt that the customer takes home. You are the POS terminal.

try_it: Add a 'daily special' that is 20% off one specific item. Add category filtering so customers can browse only Appetizers or Mains. Add a loyalty points system: every dollar spent earns 1 point, 100 points = $5 off next order. Add a split-bill feature: divide the total by N people.
tips: Store prices in cents (integers) — no floating-point rounding errors: $18.95 = 1895
Discounts apply BEFORE tax in most systems: (subtotal - discount) * tax_rate
Each cart entry needs both the MenuItem AND quantity — use parallel Vec or a wrapper struct
common_mistakes: Applying discount to total (including tax) rather than to the subtotal before tax
Forgetting to multiply item price by quantity when calculating line totals
Hardcoding discount threshold ($50) in multiple places — use a single constant or contract
